steps.observation: How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
# How Transformers Work (Conceptually)

## The Core Problem They Solve
Earlier models (like RNNs) processed text *sequentially*, word by word. This made it hard to connect distant words and slow to parallelize. Transformers process all words **simultaneously** and learn relationships between any two positions directly.

---

## Key Building Blocks

### 1. Tokens & Embeddings
- Text is split into **tokens** (words or word pieces)
- Each token becomes a **vector** (list of numbers) representing its meaning
- **Positional encoding** is added so the model knows word order

### 2. Self-Attention — The Core Idea
This is what makes transformers special. For each word, the model asks:
> *"Which other words in this sequence are most relevant to understanding me?"*

For each token, three vectors are created:
- **Query** – "What am I looking for?"
- **Key** – "What do I contain?"
- **Value** – "What information do I pass along?"

Queries are matched against all Keys to produce **attention scores**, which determine how much each token's Value influences the output. Words with high relevance get high attention weights.

**Example:** In *"The animal didn't cross the street because it was tired"* — attention helps resolve that *"it"* refers to *"animal"*, not *"street"*.

### 3. Multi-Head Attention
Rather than one attention pass, the model runs **several attention operations in parallel** (multiple "heads"), each potentially learning different types of relationships (syntax, coreference, meaning, etc.).

### 4. Feed-Forward Layers
After attention, each token passes through a **small neural network independently** — this is where more complex transformations happen.

### 5. Layer Stacking
These blocks (attention + feed-forward) are **stacked many times**. Early layers learn simple patterns; deeper layers learn abstract concepts.

---

## The Overall Flow

```
Input text
   ↓
Tokenize → Embed → Add position info
   ↓
[Self-Attention → Feed-Forward] × N layers
   ↓
Output (next token prediction, classification, etc.)
```

---

## Why It Works Well
| Property | Benefit |
|---|---|
| Parallel processing | Much faster training |
| Direct token-to-token attention | Handles long-range dependencies |
| Scalability | More data + parameters → better performance |
| General architecture | Works for text, images, audio, code |

---

## Two Main Variants
- **Encoder-only** (e.g., BERT) — reads full context, good for understanding/classification
- **Decoder-only** (e.g., GPT) — generates text left-to-right, predicting next tokens
- **Encoder-Decoder** (e.g., T5) — for translation/summarization

---

The key intuition: **attention lets every word "look at" every other word and decide what's relevant**, and doing this repeatedly across many layers builds up rich, contextual representations of meaning.
